title: To trust or not to trust: Attention-based Trust Management for LLM Multi-Agent Systems
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Different violation types activate distinct, sparse subsets of attention heads concentrated in early layers, enabling attention-based detection of untrustworthy content.
layout: 3 rows by 7 columns of heatmaps, one per violation class
description: A grid of 21 heatmaps arranged in 3 rows and 7 columns. Each column is a message class: Benign, Fact, Logic, Relevant, Bias, Quality and Clarity. In every heatmap the x-axis is attention head index (0-30) and the y-axis is layer index, with layer 0 at the top. Each map has a viridis colorbar. The top row shows raw attention scores on a 0–0.007 scale. Fact and Relevant show brighter activity in the early layers, and the Benign map is almost uniformly dark. The middle row shows binary maps in which yellow marks heads that respond to the violation. Fact, Relevant, Quality and Bias have dense yellow clusters in the top layers, while Logic and Clarity are sparser and Benign is empty. The bottom row shows a sparse binary pattern of a few yellow heads, scattered in the top layers and similar across classes. The eye goes first to the yellow blocks in the middle row.
caption: Visual analysis of multi-head attention on different violations using Llama3.1-8B, where the X-axis is the head index and the Y-axis is the layer index and each column corresponds to a different trust violation class.
abstract: Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Systems (LLM-MAS) have demonstrated strong capabilities in solving complex tasks but remain vulnerable when agents receive unreliable messages. This vulnerability stems from a fundamental gap: LLM agents treat all incoming messages equally without evaluating their trustworthiness. While some existing studies approach trustworthiness, they focus on a single type of harmfulness rather than analyze it in a holistic approach from multiple trustworthiness perspectives. We address this gap by proposing a comprehensive definition of trustworthiness inspired by human communication theory (Grice, 1975). Our definition identifies six orthogonal trust dimensions that provide interpretable measures of trustworthiness. Building on this definition, we introduce the Attention Trust Score (A -Trust), a lightweight, attention-based method for evaluating the trustworthiness of messages. We then develop a principled trust management system (TMS) for LLM -MAS that supports both message-level and agent-level trust assessments. Experiments across diverse multi-agent settings and tasks demonstrate that our TMS significantly improves robustness against malicious inputs.
